subject: blueprintSpitfire
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: Spitfire fighter plane.
Style: cyanotype blueprint.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a TypeScript module to render a Spitfire plane in cyanotype blueprint style, working out the color palette and visual elements like grid lines, white roundels, panel details, and dimension labels.

For the structure, I'll include a few key joints (body root, propeller, rudder, aileron hinges) while keeping static parts simple. I'm now working through real-world Spitfire dimensions—9.1m length, 11.23m wingspan, 3.86m height—to figure out ground clearance, wheel placement, propeller radius, and overall coordinate positioning so the model stands correctly on its landing gear.

Setting fuselage stations for the loft...

I need other joints too — rudder, elevators, ailerons, gear — with parts defaulting to the fuselage bone unless I specify otherwise. For the wings, I'm working out how to extrude an elliptical outline drawn in the plan view, figuring out which axes correspond to span, chord, and thickness.

Working out the elliptical wing shape...

I'll skip the lathe approach and instead stack two extrusions for a thickness hint — a base outline plus a shrunk inner core — placing the wing low on the fuselage and adding slight dihedral by tilting the span direction with a small y-component.

Working through the dihedral math, roughly 6° giving tip rise of about 0.56, putting the wing root near y=1.55 and tip around y=2.1. I'll also set the landing gear wheels at x=±1.9.

Modeling wheels with cylinder geometry for tires and hubs, plus a leg fairing door extruded along the gear leg. For the tail, I'm laying out the horizontal stabilizer's outline near z=-4.2 with a separate elevator joint, defining the root chord and span profile.

Setting up the elevator's hinge joint so it rotates about the trailing edge, with its own chord outline shrinking toward the tip, then moving on to extrude the vertical fin's side-view outline near the tail root.

Still plotting fin and rudder coordinates...

Working out the fin's convex outline and tip sweep, then checking the rudder hinge position against the fuselage tail cross-section so the heights line up at that z-coordinate.

Adjusting the tail end z-position so the overall fuselage length from spinner tip to tail comes out to roughly 9.15 units, then moving on to the propeller: three wooden blades radiating from a spinner cone, defining the blade outline geometry and radial/tangent axes for positioning them around the hub.

Now I'm shaping each blade's outline with a tapered width and slight curve toward the tip, giving it a thin 0.03 thickness, and considering a white tip stripe for paint detail. I'm also planning the cowl exhaust stacks -- six small ejector spikes per side near the cowl, matching the Spitfire's characteristic layout.

For the radiators, I'm positioning the port oil cooler and starboard radiator housings as chamfered boxes extruded from the side-view outline, placed beneath each wing root.

Now for the canopy I'm lofting the bubble shape from a series of station profiles running along the fuselage spine, tapering height and width front to back to sit atop the fuselage silhouette, and I'm planning to add thin white mullion stripes over the glass material to suggest the windscreen frame.

I'm deciding to skip adding a pilot figure inside and keep the canopy as a solid opaque light-blue glass volume for simplicity, since the windscreen is otherwise a flat armored panel at the front.

For the overall visual style, I'm going with a blueprint look: Prussian blue body with white linework, using a paint function that blends lighting from top to bottom while overlaying panel grid lines, rivet dots, and fine faint gridding rather than camouflage. I'm also planning white-line roundel decals on the wings and fuselage sides, plus squadron code lettering.

Skipping full dimension lines but adding text decals like "SPITFIRE Mk.I" and "SPAN 11.23 m" flat on the wing's top surface, oriented along the wing's normal to account for dihedral tilt.

I need to work out the orientation params so the text reads correctly from a viewer's perspective behind and above the plane, with the top of each letter pointing forward and readable left-to-right.

Working out the wing's slight upward slope and checking whether the text plane's tilt would cause it to clip through the wing surface given the thickness and width involved.

Computing the chord-length function and leading/trailing edge offsets for a generic wing outline helper, then defining sample stations along the span to trace the outline from root to tip.

For ailerons, I'm planning them as a separate thin extrude overlaying the outer wing's trailing edge between specific span stations, slightly raised and offset inward from the base trailing edge to represent a hinge line, each wing extruded and mirrored separately so roots meet inside the fuselage.

I realize the hinge line nearly converges with the trailing edge near the tip, making the aileron shape taper to almost nothing there. So I'm sketching the aileron as a small overlay panel spanning a short chord region near the hinge, tapering from a wider root to a thin tip.

Checking the overlay edge at u=5 stays consistent with the base trailing edge thickness so it sits just slightly proud rather than clashing. Now I'm turning to the tail wheel placement, positioning it under the rear fuselage near z=-4 and working out the strut geometry from the fuselage belly down to the ground contact point.

Confirming prop tip clearance against the spinner and fuselage height, checking that the wing root sits flush against the fuselage bottom, and sketching in finer details -- cowl panel lines, a carburetor air scoop under the nose, a windshield bump, and gun barrels along the wing leading edge.

Adding small rods for a pitot tube and antenna mast with a thin wire running to the fin tip, plus thinking about a spine fillet behind the canopy.

Now I'm planning out the decal textures: roundel rings, rudder stripes, fuselage codes like "QV-K," a squadron title block near the tail, wheel hub spokes, and stencils like "NO STEP" on the wing root.

Keeping the part count modest at around 100 for a compact but complete build. I'm defining a paint function that blends base colors by surface normal lighting, overlays major and minor grid lines along dominant axes to mimic blueprint panel lines, and adds subtle mottled noise for that uneven cyanotype look.

I'm bumping texture resolution to 2048px and thickening line width to avoid aliasing, calculating texel density against the estimated surface area to land on roughly 5mm lines at 2 texels wide. I'm simplifying to a single 0.4m grid with brighter lines plus mottle, using dominant-face mapping so it reads like a blueprint, and considering reusing the panelled kit function with customized rivet and seam settings instead of building grid lines from scratch.

I'm picking a palette of deep, mid, and light blues plus white and cyan accents, keeping total flat colors under 64, then writing a custom paint function that detects dominant axis, computes fractional UV coordinates, and draws seam lines wherever the fractional distance falls below a threshold, blended with the line color at high opacity. I'm also layering in noise-based mottling to vary the base color mix slightly across the surface.

Now I'm figuring out roundel placement on the wings, calculating wing chord dimensions and surface height at different x positions to position a 1.1m diameter circular decal correctly on the tilted wing top, planning to use a transparent-background texture plane. I'm also working out where to place the "SPITFIRE Mk I" text label near the wing root, between the fuselage and the roundel decal.

Deciding to only label one wing with "SUPERMARINE SPITFIRE Mk.I · SPAN 11.23 m" at a readable size and orientation running from the outer edge inward, while skipping underside roundels. Now I'm checking fuselage width at different z-stations to see if a roundel will fit on the side without looking cramped, since the fuselage narrows significantly toward the tail.

I'm positioning a decal of the roundel on the fuselage loft surface at around z=-2.0, sized to fit the fuselage width there, then placing squadron code letters like "QV·K" just forward of the roundel, sized small enough to match the narrower fuselage at that point.

For the opposite side's roundel, I need to think through the mirroring math carefully, since the decal's direction vector flips and I need to figure out which way is "up" and "right" relative to a viewer looking at that side from outside, so the letters read correctly rather than appearing reversed.

On the starboard side, the nose does read to the right, matching real Spitfire markings, and since it's just a viewing direction rather than a mirrored decal, I don't think I need to flip anything—the projection likely stays undistorted without an automatic mirror flag.

Now I'm working out the propeller blades, giving them a paint gradient so the tips fade to white near the edges based on radial coordinates, and shaping the spinner with a lathe profile along the axis extending past the prop hub.

I'm also figuring out how the spinner stripes get painted using height bands, and setting up the bone hierarchy so the prop joint attaches correctly at its position with the right axis direction, starting from the root fuselage part.

Now I'm planning the remaining joints: prop, rudder, elevators, ailerons, landing gear legs, tailwheel, and a canopy hinge, deciding which roles (hinge, leg) apply to each so control surfaces and gear behave correctly in the rig.

Shifting to the stabilizer geometry, I'm sketching the tail fuselage cross-section and working out the fixed stabilizer's planform points in absolute z-coordinates to define its leading and trailing edges near the tail.

Defining elevator outline...

For fuselage skin, the grid orientation should pick the dominant face, so for side surfaces I use the z,y plane. For canopy glass, I'm planning a light cyan base with frame lines at specific z-positions and a horizontal center line.

Now I'm checking that the canopy fits properly on the fuselage—adding a head fairing behind the canopy that tapers down to the fuselage top, and verifying the canopy's bottom edge stays within the fuselage profile at each station so it doesn't poke through.

The front windscreen slant should look acceptable. For the radiators, I'm placing them in boxes under the wings, matching the real Spitfire layout with the oil cooler on the left and the larger glycol radiator on the right, extruding their housing profiles along the fuselage axis.

Adding exhaust stacks and scoop placement...

I'll add three seam bands at the cowl joint, firewall, and tail, plus a small antenna mast behind the canopy connecting via a thin wire to the fin tip. Then I'm sketching the propeller hub and wheel details—tire cylinder with hub caps using the deep color texture.

Now I'm working out the hub spokes texture, mounting circular discs with white spoke lines on the outer wheel faces, and positioning the landing legs as angled rods running from the fuselage down to each wheel.

I'm deciding to skip nav lights, wing-root fillets, and flap overlays to keep things simple, and planning out color palettes for the wing surfaces—lit on top, cooler tones underneath.

I realize I can get the blueprint-style white outline look for free by checking wall normals during the extrude's paint step: where the wing's wall surface is nearly vertical, I return white, which reads as a thin edge line around the silhouette.

I'm generalizing this into an `edged()` wrapper function that checks the appropriate axis per part (y for wings/tail, x for fin/rudder, z for prop blades), then wondering if I should also add explicit white keel and ridge lines along the fuselage using a thin swept line at multiple angles around the loft.

Writing sweep and part helpers...

Adding roundel colors, title text labels with specs, and fuselage code lettering...

I'm also designing wheel hub spokes and a tail flash decal with vertical blue/white/blue stripes applied as thin plane geometry on the fin surfaces.

Now I'm setting up a generic edged-paint helper that determines wall faces by comparing the surface normal against a given thickness axis, then starting the main build script with imports for geometry helpers, randomization, and noise utilities.

Writing paint blend logic...

Writing wing outline geometry...

Checking the thickness direction cross product for each wing side to make sure the wall normal stays mostly vertical for the detection threshold to work correctly.

Now I'm working out the wing dihedral geometry and positioning the aileron hinge joint along the wing's tilted axis, computing the overlay outline points relative to the hinge offset.

I'm realizing the aileron chord should be about 20% of the local wing chord rather than running all the way back, so I'm recalculating the hinge position as trailing-edge-plus-20%-chord instead of a fixed offset.

The hinge line isn't actually straight along x since the chord and trailing-edge position change between stations, so I need to treat the hinge as a slanted joint axis between the two span points, which complicates how I extrude the aileron surface.

Working out orthogonality by crossing the hinge direction with the up vector, flipping the cross order depending on wing side so the perpendicular axis points consistently forward.

Now I'm sketching the aileron outline as a chord trailing behind the hinge line, computing the hinge length (~2.37) and the chord depth tapering from about 0.44 to 0.24-0.25, with a midpoint added for a slight curve on the trailing edge, while checking whether this aligns with the base wing's trailing edge position.

For the propeller, I'm laying out three blades spaced 120° apart around the hub, each defined by a tapered blade outline with thickness and bevel, plus a paint function that colors the blade tip white and the rest blue based on position along the blade.

I'm then adding a cylindrical ferrule at each blade root, a backplate cylinder, and lathing a spinner cone profile with banded line details near its base, finishing at the nose tip around z=4.12.

Now I'm reconciling fuselage centerline y-values along z stations to match the nose/spinner junction smoothly, adjusting the loft stations from nose to tail before capping the tail end.

I'm not sure if the loft function has distinct cap options versus sweep, so I'll skip specifying that and let it use defaults — likely producing a rounded oval cross-section for the fuselage body, passing in the station positions, widths, and heights for the loft call. I'm also considering adding an intake ring at the cowl front using a lathe-generated annulus shape.

Still writing lathe profile...

I'm planning skin surface details next — adding guide loops at specific fuselage stations and sweeping thin lines along the surface for panel lines, though I'm weighing whether tracing lines around the full circumference might be too heavy.

Letters sit on the curved surface fine, with code placement projected onto the fuselage near the roundel. I also want a fin flash marking, and now I'm starting to lay out the SVG texture for the roundel graphic.

Writing SVG code...

Skipping wing dimension labels for now. I'm sketching a small squadron code badge "QV-K" in bold white lettering, and a RAF roundel flash made of three vertical colored stripes.

Now I'm building a hub icon with a circle outline, inner white dot, spoke lines, and a dashed outer ring. Panel cards and background texture I'm leaving alone for now. I'm starting a gear-building helper function that sets wheel and top proportions scaled by size, then defines leg joints for each limb.

Continuing that, I'm wiring up the wheel joint and oleo rod/torque link parts connecting the top to the wheel axle, using a flat paint color for the gear structure, then creating a cylinder geometry for the tire mesh with a dark color.

Now I'm figuring out the wheel's tire texture and hub, adding an axle cylinder and fairing door box, checking the geometry math so the wheel bottom touches the ground properly, and starting to set up the tail wheel joint and its connecting rod.

Checking that nothing dips below ground level, then placing the radiators -- a larger one on the right and a smaller oil radiator on the left -- and verifying their vertical extents align with the wing's bottom edge.

I'm shaping the radiator profile with tapered front and back sections, then adding a simple front grille with a darker box and thin white slat details for visual texture, before moving on to the exhaust stacks.

For the exhaust stacks, I'm ray-casting along each side of the fuselage to place small cyan cylinder stubs, guarding against missed hits. I'm also considering a canopy hinge joint position to support the frame later.

Now I'm adding small details: an antenna mast with a thin wire running to the fin tip, and a pitot tube on the left wing leading edge positioned via a short rod between two coordinates — skipping side-panel hatch outlines since the paint grid already covers that.

Working out gun barrel placements...

Now I'm setting up the rudder: placing its joint at the tail, then defining an extrusion outline that flares outward and bends past the fuselage rear edge, with a control surface tab marked for painting.

I'm positioning the vertical fin and checking its geometry aligns with the rudder and stabilizer heights, then mirroring the stabilizer extrusion across the x-axis and defining joints for the fuselage spine and propeller mount.

Now I'm making sure every part has a proper bone assignment, defaulting to the fuselage unless otherwise specified, and finalizing the code structure so it returns the root. I'm also cleaning up the paint helper function, making sure unused parameters are prefixed with underscores for typing, and writing an "edged" color helper that checks surface normal thresholds to detect wall-like faces.

Still writing paint logic...

I'm defining the canopy's paint function, checking proximity to seam lines along specific z-coordinates and the central x-axis, and blending between a low and high glass color based on the normal's y-component using a smoothstep mix. I'm also picking out the glass colors themselves, a light blue base and a highlight shade.

Now I'm positioning the wing label decals and roundels, working out their world-space coordinates by tracing the wing's geometry at specific x-values along the chord, computing the corresponding z-center and offset, and setting the orientation normal and up vectors for the text placement.

I'll skip under-surface roundels, and now I'm setting up helper vectors for the aileron direction, computing endpoint positions along the wing to derive the edge direction vector.

I'm verifying the cross product logic for the yaw direction based on wing side, checking that the resulting vector stays perpendicular to the direction vector and points consistently forward for both left and right sides.

Now I'm converting the joint positions and directions to plain arrays for passing into the geometry, and planning out the bone/joint structure, prop blade placement, and bevel details before writing the full implementation.
